ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study received ethical approval from the local Institutional Review Board (#23-06-18).
Participants were randomized to either a planning, reminders, and micro-incentives intervention or a health advice control condition.

Intervention participants completed weekly phone calls to plan five 30-minute walks for the following week, received daily text messages or email reminders on planned walk days, and earned small monetary incentives upon walk completion.
Results: Forty-eight participants completed the study (retention rate: 84.2%), with high phone call compliance in both groups (intervention: 98.4%; control: 98.1%) and zero serious adverse events.
Participants were invited to participate in a virtual or in-person baseline session followed by a remote intervention (Figure 1).
table.formatted: Participants were invited to participate in a virtual or in-person baseline session followed by a remote intervention (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

table.text: Randomization allocation was concealed using REDCap and participants were blinded to the study hypotheses but investigators were not blinded to allocation.

Local participants were invited to participate in an imaging session including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalography (EEG); however, these data are not presented here due to the small n (n=10 for MRI, n=14 for EEG).
Participants Adults aged 40-80 years with a diagnosis of mild or moderate TBI between 3 months and 15 years ago were recruited via local and national digital advertisements.

Participants were required to receive a formal mild or moderate TBI diagnosis by a physician (AS) using OSU-TBI-ID questionnaire [20], requiring a direct blow or impact to the head with either loss of consciousness of 0-30 minutes (mild) or >30 minutes and <24 hours (moderate) or post-traumatic amnesia of 0-1 day (mild) or >1 day and <7days (moderate).
table.formatted: Participants were required to receive a formal mild or moderate TBI diagnosis by a physician (AS) using OSU-TBI-ID questionnaire [20], requiring a direct blow or impact to the head with either loss of consciousness of 0-30 minutes (mild) or >30 minutes and <24 hours (moderate) or post-traumatic amnesia of 0-1 day (mild) or >1 day and <7days (moderate).

table.text: Participants were encouraged (during weekly phone calls) to track their progress on the study website (sFigure 1), view completed walks and point totals.
Participants were reminded to wear their Fitbit consistently and check the study platform for weekly health tips.

First, multilevel logistic regressions predicted whether a participant completed at least one qualifying walk on a given day (46 participants, 3,750 participant-days) from the z-scored baseline scale, adjusted for age, sex, years of education, time since injury, group and study month (1-3), with a random intercept per participant; effects are odds ratios per 1 SD with 95% Wald CIs.
We recruited participants across the continental United States, with a 15% attrition rate and high compliance throughout the weekly intervention and activity tracking.

Despite intervention participants wearing their device for fewer hours per day and having fewer valid wear days than controls, they still demonstrated substantially greater walking activity, suggesting that intervention participants were removing their devices after performing bouts of physical activity.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Several limitations to this study should be considered when interpreting the results. First, this was a pilot study and therefore not powered to test overall efficacy of the intervention. Effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals and standard errors to inform the planning of a larger trial, and the study achieved only 72% power to detect the achieved effect size of the difference in walking bouts over time between groups (primary efficacy analysis). Second, participants varied considerably in time since injury, though this heterogeneity likely reflects the true diversity of the communitydwelling TBI population rather than a methodological limitation. Third, as a 12-week pilot trial, the long-term maintenance of the observed walking increases remains to be established, and future research should examine whether effects are sustained beyond the active intervention period. Fourth, the sample was not balanced by sex, with a predominance of female participants, and lacked racial and ethnic diversity, which limits the generalizability of the findings to more diverse TBI populations. Fifth, while Fitbit provided objective and continuous measurement of walking behavior, we only captured activities explicitly logged as walks, and incidental ambulatory activity or other activities (i.e. cycling or rowing) not recorded as a discrete walk event may have been missed.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "Several limitations to this study should be considered when interpreting the results. First, this was a pilot study and therefore not powered to test overall efficacy of the intervention. Effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals and standard errors to inform the planning of a larger trial, and the study achieved only 72% power to detect the achieved effect size of the difference in walking bouts over time between groups (primary efficacy analysis). Second, participants varied considerably in time since injury, though this heterogeneity likely reflects the true diversity of the communitydwelling TBI population rather than a methodological limitation. Third, as a 12-week pilot trial, the long-term maintenance of the observed walking increases remains to be established, and future research should examine whether effects are sustained beyond the active intervention period. Fourth, the sample was not balanced by sex, with a predominance of female participants, and lacked racial and ethnic diversity, which limits the generalizability of the findings to more diverse TBI populations. Fifth, while Fitbit provided objective and continuous measurement of walking behavior, we only captured activities explicitly logged as walks, and incidental ambulatory activity or other activities (i.e. cycling or rowing) not recorded as a discrete walk event may have been missed."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::
